The material was produced as ∼50 g bars by vacuum arc melting, using elements with more than 99.9% purity, and a procedure of 5 inversion and melting steps to ensure homogeneity.
The alloys were then homogenised at 1200 °C for 4 h under vacuum to minimise micro segregation.

Alloying with W, and especially the greater addition of 2 at.% W, lead to agglomeration of the precipitate phases, and a conjoined γ′-γ″ precipitate network, as opposed to distinct boundaries between the two phases.

Alloying with W, and especially the greater addition of 2 at.% W, lead to agglomeration of the precipitate phases, and a conjoined γ′-γ″ precipitate network
The addition of Co has produced considerable coarsening of the γ″ precipitates, resulting in long laths that are unconstrained by the surrounding γ′ precipitates.
Comparison of the data for each alloy revealed that there was little variation in the hardness between the 10 h and 100 h heat treatments
the increased coarsening of the γ″ precipitates, brought about by additions of Co, is a likely cause of the observed decrease in hardness

The addition of Mo and W led to substantial hardening of the alloy, potentially leading to improved mechanical properties. However, for the addition of W, this comes at the expense of the morphology of the precipitates formed in the alloy
